q: The scale shows $0.5\,\text{g}$ when empty. The mean of ten weighings of an object is $20.4\,\text{g}$, and the readings vary only between $20.3\,\text{g}$ and $20.5\,\text{g}$. Which error dominates and what is the mass of the object?
a: Systematic error dominates: the readings are close to each other, so random error is small ($\Delta m = 0.1\,\text{g}$), but the zero reading $0.5\,\text{g}$ is in every reading. The mass is $m = 20.4\,\text{g} - 0.5\,\text{g} = 19.9\,\text{g}$.

q: Why does taking the mean reduce random error but not systematic error?
a: Random error pushes in a different direction each time, so results that are too large and too small partly cancel each other in the mean. A systematic error is in the same direction in every measurement, so it is just as large in the mean too.

q: A measurement result is $t = 4.52\,\text{s} \pm 0.09\,\text{s}$. Calculate the relative error as a percentage.
a: $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta t}{\bar{t}} \cdot 100\,\% = \dfrac{0.09\,\text{s}}{4.52\,\text{s}} \cdot 100\,\% \approx 2\,\%$, one significant figure like the error estimate $0.09\,\text{s}$.
